title: Strategy
summary: Swap algorithms behind one interface when the variation is the behavior.

parts.rule: Strategy gives several interchangeable algorithms one contract. A context receives one strategy and delegates the varying calculation to it while keeping the surrounding workflow fixed. Selection usually happens outside the context through configuration, input, or dependency injection; a strategy can be an object or simply a function.
parts.why: When one class switches among growing algorithm variants, every new variant risks changing stable workflow code. Separating the algorithm makes each variant testable and lets the caller choose deliberately. The tradeoff is indirection: if there is one tiny branch and no likely variation, the switch may be the clearer design.
parts.example: Checkout always validates the cart, asks for a shipping quote, takes payment, and creates the order. Only shipping cost varies. ShippingStrategy.quote(weightKg, distanceKm) has three implementations. FlatRate returns 500 cents. WeightBased returns 200 + 75 × weightKg. CourierDistance returns 300 + 20 × distanceKm. For a parcel weighing 8 kg traveling 30 km, the results are 500, 800, and 900 cents. The merchant configuration selects WeightBased and injects it into Checkout; Checkout calls quote(8, 30) and adds 800 cents without knowing the formula. Tests run the same inputs against each strategy and separately verify that Checkout uses the returned quote once. Adding HolidayFreeShipping changes the registration list, not the payment workflow. If discounts must stack—VIP plus coupon plus seasonal—the design may need a pipeline of rules or decorators rather than selecting one mutually exclusive strategy. Also distinguish State: a caller chooses a shipping strategy, but an Order moves from Pending to Paid because lifecycle events occur. If the only rule is freeShipping ? 0 : 500 and that boolean is stable, one named function or conditional is easier to read than two classes.
parts.use: Use Strategy for pricing, ranking, routing, validation policies, compression, and other algorithms that share inputs and outputs but vary independently of the context. Define the contract around behavior, select the variant in a visible place, and test every implementation with common contract cases.
parts.refuse: Keep a direct conditional when it is short, local, and unlikely to grow. Do not create one strategy type per trivial line or bury formulas so deeply that reviewers cannot find them. Strategies must be substitutable under the same contract; if one requires unrelated inputs or changes workflow semantics, the abstraction is probably wrong. Use State when variation follows an internal lifecycle.

body:
Rule. Strategy gives several interchangeable algorithms one contract. A context receives one strategy and delegates the varying calculation to it while keeping the surrounding workflow fixed. Selection usually happens outside the context through configuration, input, or dependency injection; a strategy can be an object or simply a function.

Why it matters. When one class switches among growing algorithm variants, every new variant risks changing stable workflow code. Separating the algorithm makes each variant testable and lets the caller choose deliberately. The tradeoff is indirection: if there is one tiny branch and no likely variation, the switch may be the clearer design.

Worked example. Checkout always validates the cart, asks for a shipping quote, takes payment, and creates the order. Only shipping cost varies. ShippingStrategy.quote(weightKg, distanceKm) has three implementations. FlatRate returns 500 cents. WeightBased returns 200 + 75 × weightKg. CourierDistance returns 300 + 20 × distanceKm. For a parcel weighing 8 kg traveling 30 km, the results are 500, 800, and 900 cents. The merchant configuration selects WeightBased and injects it into Checkout; Checkout calls quote(8, 30) and adds 800 cents without knowing the formula. Tests run the same inputs against each strategy and separately verify that Checkout uses the returned quote once. Adding HolidayFreeShipping changes the registration list, not the payment workflow. If discounts must stack—VIP plus coupon plus seasonal—the design may need a pipeline of rules or decorators rather than selecting one mutually exclusive strategy. Also distinguish State: a caller chooses a shipping strategy, but an Order moves from Pending to Paid because lifecycle events occur. If the only rule is freeShipping ? 0 : 500 and that boolean is stable, one named function or conditional is easier to read than two classes.

When to use. Use Strategy for pricing, ranking, routing, validation policies, compression, and other algorithms that share inputs and outputs but vary independently of the context. Define the contract around behavior, select the variant in a visible place, and test every implementation with common contract cases.

When to refuse. Keep a direct conditional when it is short, local, and unlikely to grow. Do not create one strategy type per trivial line or bury formulas so deeply that reviewers cannot find them. Strategies must be substitutable under the same contract; if one requires unrelated inputs or changes workflow semantics, the abstraction is probably wrong. Use State when variation follows an internal lifecycle.
